footage.look: Live-action documentary realism, shot on a full-frame cinema camera, natural skin and real fabric, real dust hanging in the air, fine film grain, true-to-life colour, stunning, gallery-grade cinematography. High noon in a dusty 1880s frontier town: the sun directly overhead, a bleached pale sky, hard short shadows at the boots, heat shimmer over the ochre street, weathered dark pine storefronts.
footage.physics: Physics: every hand that touches a jar stays stuck fast to it and never comes free, the tray stays level in her two gloved hands with all six jars on it however hard anyone pulls, honey keeps dripping off the rim, her boots stay planted on the porch boards and she does not step or sway, the white veil stays down over her face the whole time, the rusted bear trap stays hooked behind her hip and never opens, nothing floats, nothing changes size, there is exactly one tray, six jars and one trap. She is a small woman in an amber-gold prairie dress and a straw beekeeper hat with the white veil down over her whole face; the customers are only ever arms, shoulders and backs in work shirts, their faces never in frame.

render.prompt: Locked-off 35 mm, static camera, no push, no zoom, no pan, one single unbroken twelve-second take from this one camera only. Start exactly from the first frame and continue the same continuous take without any cut; the camera never changes position, height or angle; there is no cutaway, no insert, no second angle, no close-up. The woman in the amber-gold prairie dress and the straw beekeeper hat, her face a soft blur behind the white veil pulled down over it, stands perfectly still on the saloon porch holding out the wooden tray of six dripping honey jars, while a man's arm in a tan shirt reaches in from the left edge, his hand closed on one jar. Big, fast, physical comedy from the very first second: he throws his whole weight backward, his shoulders, back and hat swinging into frame at the left as he heaves, both boots skidding loudly on the porch boards, and the hand stays glued to the jar with honey stretching in long ropes; at three seconds he slaps his free hand onto the edge of the tray to push himself off and that hand sticks too; at six seconds he is hanging almost horizontal off the tray, legs kicking, boots scrabbling for the boards, while she does not move a hair and the tray stays perfectly level; at nine seconds a second customer's hand reaches in from the right edge, grabs another jar, and sticks. She only tilts her veiled head a little; behind her hip the jaws of the rusted bear trap catch the light. In the last second both men hang off her tray like fish on a line while she stands serene.
